gap: No result ChatGPT got states that FranklinWH's '15-year' aPower 2 warranty is capped at 60 MWh, which is only 4,000 full 15 kWh cycles. At one full cycle a day that cap runs out in about 11 years, so the warranty is close to Tesla's 10-year unlimited-cycle Powerwall 3 term for daily solar cyclers. FranklinWH's own 'more than 10,000 cycles' claim only adds up if the average cycle uses 6 kWh or less (40%).
standout_why: I compared the three cited pages. EnergySage gives aPower 2 '15 years at 70%' with throughput 'not stated', and Powerwall 3 '10 years at 70%' with an 'unlimited-cycle warranty'. SolutionEnergy gives '15-year warranty (60 MWh)' but never turns it into cycles or years. iTechGuides publishes no warranty terms and only tells readers to 'ask for … permitted throughput or cycle count'. None of them put the two warranties on the same basis (years of daily full cycling), and none points out that 10,000 cycles is impossible at full depth.
decides: This confirms the order of ChatGPT's picks but changes how they should be framed. For a home that cycles the battery daily for solar self-consumption, the warranty advantage ChatGPT gave FranklinWH ('15-year warranty') shrinks to about 11 vs 10 years, and the remaining difference is capacity (15 vs 13.5 kWh) and continuous power (10 vs 11.5 kW, which favours Tesla). For a backup-only household that rarely cycles, FranklinWH's 15-year term does hold.

findings.label: Throughput cap converted to full cycles and years
findings.value: 4,000 full cycles; about 11.0 years at one full cycle a day
findings.source_title: FranklinWH aPower 2 home battery backup (maker product page)
findings.note: My arithmetic from the maker's figures: 60,000 kWh ÷ 15 kWh = 4,000 full-capacity cycles, and 4,000 ÷ 365 = 10.96 years. For '10,000 cycles' to fit inside 60 MWh, the average cycle has to be 6 kWh or less (40% of 15 kWh). So the warranty ends at whichever comes first: 15 years, or about 11 years of daily full cycling.
